_comment: THE HOOK SHEET, REGENERATED. Ordered by Jafar on 22 September, after the
first check of the approved sheet against the research and canon:
'The sheet is regenerated before anything else is matched to it. Through
the image lane, from the research and canon rather than the old prompt,
at a resolution where a shopfront's detail is evidence, at least four
times the current panel size.'
WHY A NEW PROMPT AND NOT A PATCHED ONE. The approved sheet's prompt is
CODEX'S PROMPT, translated: compare-hook-2026-09-09-pass2.json records
its source as origin/art/atlas-01 concept-prompts.json key 'hook', 1599
chars, sha256 53408df5..., and says in terms that only the 'not a ...'
clauses were moved into the negative channel. Three of the four
contradictions the audit found were therefore COMMANDED, not invented:
- 'Mickey's a SMALL SINGLE 6m-wide two-storey PUB ... maroon fascia
MICKEY'S' - the prompt asked for a pub. D19 made it a minicab office
on 14 September, five days after that prompt ran.
- 'ONLY TWO PIECES OF LETTERING IN THE WHOLE SHEET ... every other
shopfront fascia is plain unlettered PAINTED TIMBER' - the prompt
asked for unlettered timber fronts, which is why there is not one
metal shopfront and not one shop sign on the sheet, against D01, D06
and R05's photograph.
- 'inland town gently rising behind' produced a wooded hillside with
villas, where the bible expresses the rise with contour-following
terraces and retaining walls.
Only the narrowboats were the model disobeying: the old prompt said 'a
commercial cargo basin' and its negative already carried 'pleasure
marina, yacht, leisure moorings, pontoon'. That one needs the positive
to NAME the craft rather than only forbid the wrong ones.
SO EVERY SENTENCE BELOW IS WRITTEN FROM A NAMED SOURCE, and the source
is in the item's own 'governed_by' so the next person can check it
rather than trust it.
THE LANE REFUSED THE FIRST WRITING OF THIS FILE AND WAS RIGHT TWICE.
1. Every 'no sun', 'no people', 'none identifiable' and 'not a pub' sat
in the POSITIVE prompt, and the lane's own note says why that is a
fault rather than a style preference: a diffusion model reads the
noun and draws it - 'that is what put a sign board on
wall_soot_brick'. They are said positively now, or they were already
in the negative and are simply gone from the positive.
2. The negatives named 'beer' and 'brewery' - forbidden tokens, because
D18 bars alcohol from every frame and the check bans NAMING it at
all, in either channel. Dropped; 'pub, public house, inn, tavern'
carry the same exclusion without naming the drink.
THE LIBRARY'S OWN CLAUSE, COPIED VERBATIM from tools/imagegen/prompts.json
rather than rewritten. build_prompt refuses any prompt whose clause does
not contain 'no trade marks', and a re-worded clause is exactly the kind
of near-miss that passes a human read and fails the guard - which is what
happened here on the first attempt.
IT ALSO FORBIDS ALCOHOL IN FRAME, which suits this batch: D19 made
Mickey's a minicab office and canon says other pubs are facade only,
never entered for drink.
content_rules.rules_clause: invented fictional shop name only, no real company names, no real brand logos, no trade marks, no real person, no recognisable faces, no celebrity likeness, no alcohol and no gambling anywhere in frame, nothing poured or consumed, no games of chance, nobody under eighteen and no school in use, nothing sexual
content_rules.why: Every 1980s British advert and packet is still in copyright, and trade mark was the only claim Getty won in [2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch). Canon says the same: every brand, band, club, product, weapon and vehicle is fictional.

_comment: framing_required is copied verbatim from tools/imagegen/prompts.json,
as the 9 September comparison copied it, and for the same reason: it is
the check build_prompt actually runs.
by_kind.concept.prefix DIFFERS FROM THE 9 SEPTEMBER ONE and has to. That
batch made a POSTER, so 'the whole board filling the frame edge to edge'
described what it was. These items are PANELS - one photograph each, at
the resolution a poster cannot carry - so the phrase that satisfies the
check without describing a board is the one below.
suffix is PRESENT AND EMPTY, because omitting it inherits a default that
ends 'one single flat surface', which is a board again.
style.framing_required: filling the frame edge to edge

concept.prefix: the view filling the frame edge to edge,

defaults.sampler: unset - sd-cli picks its model-specific default
_comment: steps and cfg are the library's measured settings for Z-Image-Turbo
and are unchanged. cfg 1.0 is where this distilled model is measured
and where the negative channel is inert - which is why every negative
below is a backstop and nothing depends on it.

size_note: THE RESOLUTION, AND WHY IT IS SHAPED THIS WAY. The approved sheet is a
688 x 1024 POSTER whose street panel is only 617 x 326 - and a shopfront
in that panel is about 60 px wide, which is why the audit had to say
that anything under four pixels on it is not evidence of anything.
Jafar: 'at a resolution where a shopfront's detail is evidence, at least
four times the current panel size.' So the PANELS ARE GENERATED AS
PANELS, full frame each, instead of as two stamps inside a poster:
street  2048 x 1088 - 1.88, the panel's own aspect, 3.3x linear and
11x the area of 617 x 326. A 6 m shopfront in it is about
shopfront study 1536 x 1024 - one bay at arm's length, because the
thing the research is strongest on (frame sections, strip
light, tiled stallriser, stacked goods) is the thing no
street view at any resolution resolves.
basin   1536 x 1024 - the top panel's subject, on its own.
The poster is assembled from the panels afterwards if he wants one;
assembling loses nothing, and generating a poster loses the resolution.

items.binds_to: CANDIDATE FOR THE HOOK SHEET'S STREET PANEL - not shipped, not bound, pass 1 of 3. Jafar 2026-09-22.
governed_by: canon.md: Quay Street in the Hook; MICKEY'S IS A MINICAB OFFICE (D19); a rank outside; other pubs are facade only, never entered for drink; 1988-1992, late-analog; every brand fictional.
TOWN-FORM-BIBLE rule 3: continuous party-wall runs, the source street's 6 m modules intact.
TOWN-FORM-BIBLE D06 and R05: Hook shops receive metal frames, practical light fittings and repair patches within older masonry - AMONG older fronts, not instead of them.
R09 (Spring Bank, Hull, 1989): casual printed tops, trainers, lightweight jackets, metal shopfronts, slab paving, carriageway markings, parked cars.
TOWN-FORM-BIBLE rule 6: flat low harbour ground, then a deliberate inland rise expressed by CONTOUR-FOLLOWING TERRACES, RETAINING WALLS and STAIR SHORTCUTS - not a wooded hill.
TOWN-FORM-BIBLE era: grime follows water paths, hands, deliveries and heating; it does not cover every surface equally.
production/specs/vignette-scene.json: the street's own fascia names - MICKEY'S, FISH MARKET, RITA'S, STEAM LAUNDRY.
items.prompt: Use case: historical-scene. One photoreal pedestrian eye-height concept panel for LEDGER, the fictional British port town Meridian, an ordinary wet overcast weekday in 1990. Camera 1.6 m standing in the carriageway at the south end of Quay Street looking north: 6 m wet asphalt with a crowned camber and white centre line, double yellow lines both sides, 2 m stone flag pavement each side with a kerb. Both sides are continuous two-storey red and soot brick party-wall terraces in 6 m bays under a 35 degree slate roof with party-wall chimney stacks, varied roof heights, flat brick arches over tall narrow white two-over-two sash windows upstairs. On the right the first bay is MICKEY'S, a MINICAB OFFICE: a plain shopfront with a wide plate window, a card in the glass, a counter and a wall radio visible inside, a maroon fascia reading MICKEY'S in plain painted capitals, and TWO ORDINARY SALOON CARS WAITING NOSE TO TAIL AT THE KERB DIRECTLY OUTSIDE IT as a cab rank. The next bay north is a SEPARATE shop in its own 6 m module with its own party wall and its own fascia reading FISH MARKET. THE PARADE IS A MIXTURE OF OLD AND REFITTED FRONTS, which is the point: two bays have 1970s and 1980s METAL SHOPFRONTS, slim dark aluminium frames, a cold fluorescent strip burning inside behind the glass, goods stacked against the window, a patterned glazed tile stallriser and brick repair patches around the new opening; the others keep older painted timber fronts with pilasters and painted stallrisers. EVERY SHOP CARRIES A SIGN: fascias reading RITA'S and STEAM LAUNDRY in plain painted capitals, a hand-lettered card in one window, a small enamel notice on a blank wall. Grime where water and hands put it - soot streaks under gutters, a dark splashed metre at the foot of every wall, clean patches where doors are used - uneven and patchy across the fronts. Three or four ordinary people at different distances in 1990 British high street clothes, casual printed tops, trainers, lightweight jackets, seen from behind or too far off for a face to read. One small dark saloon parked further up. At the far end of the street the ground rises inland into CONTOUR-FOLLOWING BRICK TERRACES STEPPING UP THE SLOPE BEHIND STONE RETAINING WALLS, pale and soft in the haze. Photoreal throughout, photographic material plausibility, soft directionless overcast light under a flat white sky.

items.prompt: Use case: historical-scene. One photoreal establishing concept panel for LEDGER, the fictional British port town Meridian, an ordinary wet overcast weekday in 1990. A small enclosed working dock basin seen from a low quayside: STEEL-HULLED WORKING COASTAL CRAFT MOORED AGAINST THE WALL - a blunt-bowed inshore fishing boat with a wheelhouse aft, derrick and stacked fish boxes on deck, and beyond it a low flat-decked coastal cargo barge with a hatch coaming, both scuffed and workaday and rust-streaked. A straight coursed stone quay wall with heavy iron mooring rings and a chain edge, bollards, coiled rope, a stack of pallets and empty fish boxes on the quay. Two-storey and three-storey red and soot brick warehouses stand straight out of the water along the far side, small square loading doors with hoist beams, corrugated sheet repairs, a DISTANT LATTICE DOCKSIDE CRANE against the sky. Behind them the ground rises inland into CONTOUR-FOLLOWING BRICK TERRACES STEPPING UP THE SLOPE BEHIND STONE RETAINING WALLS, pale and soft in the haze. A lorry backed up to a warehouse door, two workers in ordinary 1990 workwear, seen from behind and too far off for a face to read. Dark water with a little chop on it. Photoreal throughout, photographic material plausibility, soft directionless overcast light under a flat white sky.

items.binds_to: CANDIDATE FOR THE HOOK SHEET'S STREET PANEL - pass 2 of 3, written from pass 1's faults.
governed_by: PASS 2, written from what PASS 1 actually produced rather than from the same idea again.

FAULT 1, the worst: Mickey's came back as a DELICATESSEN - bottles, jars and packaged goods in the window, a man behind a counter - and with NO RANK outside. D19 makes it a minicab office and canon gives it 'a rank outside'. The prompt named it a minicab office in one clause among thirty; it is now the SUBJECT, named first, described by its contents (radio, fare book, waiting chairs, a hand-lettered card) rather than by its trade name, and the rank is three cars and a driver.

FAULT 2: not one metal shopfront appeared, though two were asked for. A refit described in the middle of a long period-terrace passage loses to the terrace. The metal front is now the NEAREST bay, closest to the camera, described before the terrace behind it.

FAULT 3: every fascia carried garbled lettering - MIC?KIY, FIT?ON M?KER. Z-Image at 8 steps cannot spell more than one sign. The old Codex prompt's 'ONLY TWO PIECES OF LETTERING' clause existed for this reason and dropping it was my error. One legible piece now - a hand-lettered card - and the rest are 'too far off and too rain-streaked for their lettering to be read'.
FAULT 4: two CCTV cameras appeared on the wall. canon.md: 'CCTV rare: the bank, and a second site that is Jafar's to name'. Added to the negative.

FAULT 5: the street read as a prosperous market town - clean brick, fresh paint, no grime. The bible says grime follows water paths, hands, deliveries and heating. Said far more concretely now: soot under every gutter, a dark splashed metre at the foot of every wall, flaking paint, rust, patched pointing.

AND THE SHOPFRONT STUDY FAILED THE SAME WAY, which is what changed this clause. It produced the tile stallriser, the strip light and the stacked goods - R05's own details, all three - inside a PAINTED TIMBER FRAME with pilasters and a moulded cornice. 'Metal shopfront' as an adjective on a shopfront loses to every other word in the sentence. It is described as the OBJECT now: a flat aluminium window unit set against the brick, with the timber parts named as absent by naming what is there instead.
items.prompt: Use case: historical-scene. One photoreal pedestrian eye-height concept panel for LEDGER, the fictional British port town Meridian, a wet overcast working weekday in 1990. THE SUBJECT IS A MINICAB OFFICE AND ITS RANK, and it fills the right half of the frame: MICKEY'S CARS, a small ground-floor MINICAB OFFICE in a red brick terrace - a wide plain plate glass window with a HAND-LETTERED CARD taped inside reading MICKEY'S, a bare counter behind the glass with a two-way RADIO SET and a hardbacked FARE BOOK open on it, a wall clock, a strip light, a couple of moulded plastic chairs against the side wall for people waiting, and a plain painted fascia over the window. THREE ORDINARY DARK SALOON CARS WAIT NOSE TO TAIL AT THE KERB DIRECTLY OUTSIDE IT as a taxi rank, one driver leaning on a wing with his arms folded. THE BAY NEAREST THE CAMERA, on the same side and closer, HAS HAD ITS OLD SHOPFRONT TORN OUT AND REPLACED BY A FLAT ALUMINIUM WINDOW UNIT, the way a 1980s post office or bookmaker was refitted: a plain rectangular frame of thin dark metal sections set FLAT against the bare brickwork, metal top to bottom and edge to edge, one wide sheet of plate glass divided by two slim metal glazing bars, a matching flat metal door beside it with a long metal push bar, a cold white fluorescent tube burning inside just behind the glass, cardboard boxes and stacked goods pushed against the window from inside, a PATTERNED GLAZED TILE STALLRISER below the glass, and raw new brick repair patches around the opening where the old front was cut away. Behind and beyond them the street runs on: a continuous two-storey red and soot brick party-wall terrace in repeated 6 m bays under a 35 degree slate roof, party-wall chimney stacks, varied roof heights, flat brick arches over tall narrow white two-over-two sash windows upstairs, and further shop bays whose painted fascia boards are too far off and too rain-streaked for their lettering to be read. 6 m wet asphalt carriageway with a crowned camber, a white centre line, double yellow lines both sides, 2 m stone flag pavement each side with a kerb. HEAVILY WORN AND SOOTED: black soot streaks running down the brick under every gutter and beside every cast iron downpipe, a dark splashed metre at the foot of every wall from pavement splash, flaking paint on the joinery, rust stains, patched pointing - uneven and patchy across the fronts. Two or three ordinary working people at different distances in 1990 British clothes, seen from behind or too far off for a face to read. At the far end the ground rises inland into CONTOUR-FOLLOWING BRICK TERRACES STEPPING UP THE SLOPE BEHIND STONE RETAINING WALLS, pale and soft in the haze. Photoreal throughout, photographic material plausibility, soft directionless overcast light under a flat white sky.
